title: Il Milione: Venice to Cathay and Back Through the Book of Marvels
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Fathers' Road and the Birth of a Son

stops.name: Venice, born in the parish of San Giovanni Grisostomo
stops.campa: In the parish of San Giovanni Grisostomo, hard by the Rialto, a son is born to Nicolò Polo's household while Nicolò himself is a world away, already deep in the Volga steppe with his brother Maffeo. The house stands in the little court that will one day be called Corte del Milione for his sake, though no one yet knows it. His mother does not live to see him grown; he is raised among aunts and the ledgers of a merchant house that trades as far as Constantinople and the Black Sea, waiting on news that does not come for years.
suggested_refs: The Veneto-Byzantine arch of the Corte del Milion, all that survives of the Polo family house
sources: Il Milione / The Travels of Marco Polo, Prologue (Yule-Cordier translation)

stops.name: Constantinople, the fathers' venture east
stops.campa: Nicolò and Maffeo Polo, merchants of Venice long settled in Constantinople's Venetian quarter, read the shifting fortune of the Latin Empire and convert their wares into a portable treasure of jewels. They sail into the Black Sea and up the rivers of the Golden Horde, trading as they go, meaning only to turn a profit among the Tartars and come home within a season. Neither yet imagines the road will run nine years and carry them to the far side of the earth, to a Khan who has never seen a Latin Christian and very much wishes to.
suggested_refs: The Venetian quarter of medieval Constantinople, starting point of the family's fortune

stops.name: Sarai on the Volga, the court of Barka Khan
stops.campa: The brothers come to Sarai on the lower Volga, seat of Barka, khan of the western Tartars, and find their jewels so prized that they double their fortune within the year. They linger a year more, learning the roads and the tongues of the steppe, until war breaks out between Barka and his cousin Hulagu of Persia, closing the road home behind them. Turned away from Constantinople, they push east instead, choosing to wait out the war among the Tartars of Transoxiana rather than sit idle on a shut frontier with a fortune growing restless in their saddlebags.
suggested_refs: The ruins of Sarai Batu on the lower Volga, capital of the Golden Horde

stops.name: Bukhara, three years waiting out the war
stops.campa: Barred from turning home by the war of the khans, Nicolò and Maffeo settle three years in Bukhara, a handsome city under Tartar rule, trading and learning the Tartar tongue and manners until they pass for men half of the steppe themselves. Here an embassy bound for the court of the Great Khan Kublai, brother of the warring Hulagu, finds them and, delighted to bring along Latins who speak Tartar, invites them east, an invitation the brothers take for providence, not knowing it will carry them to the farthest court on earth and back again with a charge from an emperor.
suggested_refs: The old citadel and minarets of Bukhara on the Silk Road

stops.name: Khanbaliq: before the Great Khan, the golden tablet
stops.campa: A year's riding brings the brothers to the court of Kublai, Great Khan of the Tartars, who has never before set eyes on Latin Christians and questions them a full day about the Pope, the Roman Church, and the princes of the West. He receives them with high honor, and at their leave-taking entrusts them with a golden tablet a foot long, commanding safe conduct, lodging, and horses throughout his dominions, together with a charge for the Pope: send a hundred wise men learned in the Christian law, and oil from the lamp that burns before the Holy Sepulchre at Jerusalem.
suggested_refs: The Mongol paiza (golden tablet of safe conduct) granted by Kublai Khan

stops.name: Venice: the fathers' return, a son fifteen years grown
stops.campa: Nine years gone, Nicolò and Maffeo land again at Venice to find the world remade: Nicolò's wife is dead, and the boy left an infant is a youth of fifteen, sharp-eyed and quick with figures, grown up on his father's absence and his father's trade. There is no pope to receive the Khan's golden tablet and its charge, for the Holy See stands vacant these two years past a wrangling conclave at Viterbo. The brothers wait at home as merchants again, the boy Marco listening hungrily to every word of Cathay, until the Church can give them an answer worth carrying back.
suggested_refs: Niccolò and Maffeo Polo's homecoming, as told in the Prologue of Il Milione

segments.name: Acre and the Errand of the Sepulchre

stops.name: Venice, the three Polos depart
stops.campa: Two years the papal chair stands empty, and the brothers will wait no longer: they sail for the Levant with the seventeen-year-old Marco at their side, meaning to reach Acre, take what answer the papal legate there can give, and press on to the Khan regardless of Rome. It is the boy's first crossing of the sea that has carried his father's whole working life, and he goes as a son learning the family trade: bales, exchange, the weighing of pearls, with no warning yet that he sails toward twenty-four years and three-quarters of the known world.
suggested_refs: The departure of the three Polos from Venice, as told in the Prologue of Il Milione

stops.name: Acre, the letters of the newly elected pope
stops.campa: At Acre the Polos learn that their friend the papal legate, Teobaldo Visconti, has at last been raised to the chair of Peter as Gregory X. They return to him for proper letters and companions before pressing on; the new pope, unable to spare the hundred teachers Kublai asked for, gives them two Dominican friars instead, with letters commending the Polos and their errand to the Great Khan. The friars will turn back within weeks at the first rumor of war in Armenia; the Polos, papal letters in hand and the friars' mission now theirs alone, do not.
suggested_refs: The Franciscan-Dominican mission house of crusader Acre, gateway of the papal embassy
sources: Encyclopedia.com, 'The Journeys of Marco Polo and Their Impact'

stops.name: Jerusalem, the oil of the Holy Sepulchre lamp
stops.campa: Before recrossing into Asia the Polos ride up to Jerusalem to fulfill the one plain charge the Khan laid on them himself: oil from the lamp that burns day and night before the Holy Sepulchre, which the Tartar lord has heard is the most sacred substance of the Christians and desires above the hundred wise men the Pope could not send. They take their portion from the lamp of the Resurrection and carry it east in a small vessel, past deserts and mountains and years of road, until it is set at last before Kublai's own throne at distant Khanbaliq.
suggested_refs: The Edicule of the Holy Sepulchre and its perpetual lamp, Church of the Holy Sepulchre
sources: Encyclopedia.com, 'The Journeys of Marco Polo and Their Impact'

stops.name: Ayas (Laiazzo), onward into Asia Minor
stops.campa: From Jerusalem they take ship again for Ayas, the Genoese and Venetian trading port of the Cilician coast, gateway between the sea and the whole overland road to Cathay. Here the two Dominican friars, hearing of Baibars the Mameluke's war raging through Armenia, lose heart and turn back to Acre, leaving the papal letters in the Polos' keeping. The three Venetians go on alone: Nicolò, Maffeo, and the boy Marco, into the mountains of Lesser Armenia and toward Greater Armenia and Persia beyond, the friars' abandoned errand now entirely their own to carry.
suggested_refs: The medieval port of Ayas (Laiazzo), now Yumurtalık on the Gulf of İskenderun

stops.name: Tabriz, the noble city of Persia
stops.campa: Through Greater Armenia, Georgia, Mosul and Baghdad the road brings them down into Persia to Tabriz, a great and noble city whose weavers work silk and cloth of gold and whose bazaars, the jewellers' most of all, dazzle Marco's eye with stones brought from India and beyond. Latin traders, Genoese chiefly, throng the market as he will one day write. It is a Persia scarcely two generations past the Ganja of the poet Nizami, whose Five Treasures were still being copied and sung in these same Ilkhanid lands the Polos now cross as strangers and merchants both.
stops.quote: Merchandize is brought thither from India, Baudas, Cremesor, and many other regions... and it is also a great market for precious stones.
stops.quote_source: The Travels of Marco Polo, Book I, ch. IV (Yule-Cordier translation)
suggested_refs: The jewellers' bazaar of Tabriz, dazzling Marco's eye per his own account
nizami.journey.json, the same Ilkhanid Persia a half-century after Nizami

stops.name: Hormuz, the ships not worth trusting
stops.campa: Down through Persia's spice-roads and the kingdom of Kerman the Polos reach Hormuz on the Gulf, meaning to take ship straight for India and the coast of Cathay. But the vessels of Hormuz are sewn, not nailed: planks stitched with twine of husk-fibre and caulked with fish-oil, without iron, so that a rough sea shakes them apart and drowns the merchants aboard. Nicolò judges the risk too great for the boy and the goods alike, and the three turn back north into Persia to find the long land road instead, a choice that will cost two more years of desert and mountain.
stops.quote: Their ships are wretched affairs, and many of them get lost; for they have no iron fastenings, and are only stitched together with twine made from the husk of the Indian nut.
stops.quote_source: The Travels of Marco Polo, Book I, ch. XVIII (Yule-Cordier translation)
suggested_refs: The stitched, unnailed coastal dhows of the medieval Hormuz trade

segments.name: The Silk Road: Persia to the Roof of the World

stops.name: Kerman, the desert of salt and poison springs
stops.campa: Back through Kerman, province of turquoise and steel, the Polos fill skins of goat-hide with water and turn east into the Dasht-e Lut, the desert the Persians call the Plain of Emptiness, where the springs run bitter with salt or poisoned with copper and a careless mouthful can kill a man within a day. Seven days they cross it, resting at a walled town before the ordeal to rest men and beasts, then eight days more of gravel and dead ground before green country and the first villages of Khorasan rise on the far side of the waste.
suggested_refs: The Dasht-e Lut, the 'Desert of Emptiness' Marco Polo crossed east of Kerman

stops.name: Balkh, the ruined city of Alexander
stops.campa: The road climbs into ancient Balkh, a great and splendid city once, Marco notes, until the Tartars sacked and half-ruined it; the natives still say Alexander the Great took a wife here, a daughter of Darius, and point to broken marble as proof. Wolves and lions are said to prowl the wasted quarters by night. From Balkh the country begins visibly to climb: orchards give way to bare hills, the air thins, and the caravan turns south and east toward Badakhshan, where the mountains that will not let them down again for months on end begin in earnest.
stops.quote: Balc is a noble city and a great, though it was much greater in former days. But the Tartars and other nations have greatly ravaged and destroyed it.
stops.quote_source: The Travels of Marco Polo, Book I, ch. XXVIII (Yule-Cordier translation)
suggested_refs: The ruins of ancient Balkh, the 'noble city' half-destroyed by the Tartars

stops.name: Badakhshan, the mountains of ruby and healthful air
stops.campa: Badakhshan yields the finest rubies in the world, mined by the king's own license from a mountain called Syghinan on pain of death for any who dig without leave, and lapis lazuli besides, ground to the blue of heaven for painters' pigment. The mountain air, Marco writes with a traveler's relief, is so wholesome that a man sick in the plains climbs two days into these heights and is cured, sound within three days more, a note he sets down, some readers guess, from his own convalescence here after the fevers of the long lowland roads behind him.
stops.quote: It is in this province that those fine and valuable gems the Balas Rubies are found... There is also in the same country another mountain, in which azure is found; 'tis the finest in the world.
stops.quote_source: The Travels of Marco Polo, Book I, ch. XXIX (Yule-Cordier translation)
suggested_refs: The ruby mines of Badakhshan, licensed by the king on pain of death
sources: erenow.org, 'Marco Polo: From Venice to Xanadu'

stops.name: The Pamir, forty days on the roof of the world
stops.campa: Twelve days up a river gorge and then onto the Pamir itself, a plain the natives call Bam-i-Dunya, the Roof of the World, where no bird flies for the thinness of the air and no fire burns bright or cooks food well at such height, and the cold is bitter even at high summer. Twelve days more of this desolate tableland, without house or habitation, before the road descends at last toward Kashgar, the hardest single stretch of the whole outward road, by Marco's own account, and the gate into the Tartar-held towns of the true Silk Road.
stops.quote: The plain is called Pamier, and you ride across it for twelve days together, finding nothing but a desert without habitations or any green thing, so that travellers are obliged to carry with them whatever they have need of.
stops.quote_source: The Travels of Marco Polo, Book I, ch. XXXII (Yule-Cordier translation)
suggested_refs: The Pamir plateau, 'Bam-i-Dunya', the Roof of the World

segments.name: Kashgar to Shangdu: the Desert of Spirits

stops.name: Kashgar
stops.campa: Kashgar sits fat and fertile after the Pamir's hunger, its orchards of cotton, flax, and vine watering the caravans before the last, worst desert. Nestorian Christians keep their own churches here beside the mosques, a reminder that the road to Cathay is not only a Tartar road but a Christian one too, laid down by merchants and monks centuries before the Polos rode it. Marco lingers over the local reputation for sharp dealing and usury he lays on the Kashgaris, the merchant's habitual eye for who can be trusted on the next long stage of the road ahead.
suggested_refs: The old Silk Road caravan city of Kashgar, oasis before the Taklamakan

stops.name: Yarkand
stops.campa: Yarkand offers little the canon dwells on save its people's poor eyesight, which Marco blames on the water and the diet, and the goitres common in the throats of those who drink it, one of the small clinical asides that fill his book between princes and marvels. The caravan rests and resupplies for the harder ground ahead: Khotan's jade rivers first, then the true desert, the Lop, where the road narrows to single file between dunes that swallow whole parties who wander from the line of footprints and bleached bone marking the only safe way through.
suggested_refs: The oasis town of Yarkand on the southern rim of the Taklamakan

stops.name: Khotan, the jade rivers
stops.campa: Khotan's two rivers run down from the mountains carrying jade in their gravel beds, white and green stone that Chinese buyers prize above gold and that local diggers wade the shallows by moonlight to gather before the current shifts it downstream. The province is rich in cotton, grain, and vineyards, its people already subject to the Great Khan, a full eight days short of the true wilderness. Beyond Khotan the settled world gives out; the road threads a chain of small oasis-towns and then simply stops at the ragged edge of the Desert of Lop.
suggested_refs: The jade-bearing rivers of Khotan, gathered by moonlight per Marco's account

stops.name: The Desert of Lop, voices of spirits in the sands
stops.campa: A month across the Desert of Lop, water found only at rare and bitter wells, and Marco records what the guides swear is true: a straggler behind his company, riding by night, will hear his own name called and the tramp of a following troop, and following the voice will be led from the road and never found again; and that not by night alone but even at noon the air fills with drums and clashing arms and many instruments, though no living thing stands in sight for a hundred miles. Travelers hang bells on their beasts and mark cairns to hold the line.
stops.quote: Even in the day-time one hears those spirits talking. And sometimes you shall hear the sound of a variety of musical instruments, and still more commonly the sound of drums.
stops.quote_source: The Travels of Marco Polo, Book I, ch. XXXIX (Yule-Cordier translation)
suggested_refs: The Desert of Lop's haunted crossing, the singing sands of the western Gobi
sources: thehistorianshut.com, 'Marco Polo and the Singing Sands of Xinjiang'

stops.name: Ganzhou, a year among the idol-worshippers
stops.campa: Out of the Lop into Tangut country and the city of Ganzhou, the Polos halt a full year: trade, Marco says plainly, kept them, though the delay also lets Nicolò and Maffeo mend their fortune before the last leg to court. Here for the first time the travelers meet in numbers the Buddhist and Nestorian communities of the Tartar borderlands side by side, temples of gilded idols and Christian crosses within a bowshot of each other, the first hint of the vast religious tolerance Marco will find astonishing at Kublai's own court further east.
suggested_refs: The Buddhist cave temples and Nestorian crosses of the Ganzhou corridor

stops.name: Shangdu (Xanadu), arrival at the summer court of Kublai Khan
stops.campa: Three and a half years from Acre, the Polos ride into Shangdu, Kublai's summer capital, where a marble palace gilt and painted with beasts and birds stands inside a walled park of fountains and grazing deer, and beside it a whole pavilion of gilded and lacquered cane that can be taken down, cane and cord and all, and carried wherever the Emperor commands. Nicolò presents the golden tablet and the oil of the Sepulchre; Kublai receives them, and the young Marco, twenty-one now, kneels with his father and uncle, unaware he has just entered the seventeen years that will make his name outlast every court here.
stops.quote: There is at this place a very fine marble Palace, the rooms of which are all gilt and painted with figures of men and beasts and birds... inside the Park there are fountains and rivers and brooks, and beautiful meadows, with all kinds of wild animals.
stops.quote_source: The Travels of Marco Polo, Book I, ch. LXI (Yule-Cordier translation)
suggested_refs: The ruins of Shangdu (Xanadu) in Inner Mongolia, and Coleridge's poem it inspired centuries later

segments.name: Seventeen Years in the Service of the Great Khan

stops.name: Khanbaliq, taken into the Khan's own service
stops.campa: At the winter capital of Khanbaliq, Kublai finds in the young Venetian a gift for languages and a merchant's eye for the odd fact that pleases him more than any formal report, and takes Marco into personal service, sending him on missions through the provinces of Cathay and Manzi that other envoys narrate dryly and that Marco returns from full of tales of custom, marvel, and revenue, exactly what the Khan wants of him. He learns Mongol and at least one Chinese dialect, some sources claim four tongues in all, and rises within a few years to posts of genuine trust.
suggested_refs: The Yuan winter capital of Khanbaliq (Cambaluc), on the site of modern Beijing

stops.name: Khanbaliq: the bark of trees that passes for money, the post-roads
stops.campa: Two wonders of Kublai's rule strike Marco harder than any temple: paper money, stamped with the Khan's own seal from the inner bark of the mulberry and passed current through the length of the empire as though it were gold, refused by no man on pain of death; and the post-roads, three hundred paces wide, planted with shade trees, strung every twenty-five miles with a post-house of four hundred horses, so that a courier belted with warning bells can cover two hundred and fifty miles between one sunrise and the next across the whole breadth of Cathay.
stops.quote: All these pieces of paper are issued with as much solemnity and authority as if they were of pure gold or silver... and indeed everybody takes them readily, for wheresoever a person may go throughout the Great Kaan's dominions he shall find these pieces of paper current.
stops.quote_source: The Travels of Marco Polo, Book II, ch. XXIV (Yule-Cordier translation)
suggested_refs: Kublai Khan's mulberry-bark paper money, the world's first state fiat currency in Marco's account
sources: historyofinformation.com, 'Marco Polo Describes the Issue of Paper Money'

stops.name: Yangzhou, three years' governance
stops.campa: The Khan sets Marco to govern the great city of Yangzhou for three years, one of twenty-seven cities under its jurisdiction, so the canon claims, though later scholars find no Chinese record of a foreign governor by that name in these years and guess at some lesser office dressed up in the telling. True governor or trusted officer of the Khan's revenue, Marco walks streets of silk-weavers and salt-merchants that a memorial hall to him stands in today, the one Chinese city that claims him for its own civic memory rather than merely a place he passed through.
suggested_refs: The Marco Polo Memorial Hall at Yangzhou, the city that claims his governorship
sources: Wikipedia, 'Marco Polo' (on scholarly doubt of the governorship)

stops.name: Karajang (Yunnan), the mission to the western marches
stops.campa: Sent far southwest into Karajang, the province the Chinese call Yunnan, Marco crosses country of tigers and gold panned from riverbeds and cowrie shells passing for small coin, and describes with a naturalist's frankness the black-toothed, tattoo-legged people of Zardandan and the strange custom by which a new father takes to his bed forty days while his wife rises at once to nurse both him and the newborn child. It is the farthest south the canon sends him, on the edge of Burma and the elephant-kingdoms, before the road turns him back toward the capital and, eventually, toward the sea.
stops.quote: In this country gold-dust is found in great quantities; that is to say in the rivers and lakes, whilst in the mountains gold is also found in pieces of larger size... And for small change they use porcelain shells.
stops.quote_source: The Travels of Marco Polo, Book II, ch. XLVIII-XLIX (Yule-Cordier translation)
suggested_refs: The tattooed 'Zardandan' peoples of the Yunnan borderlands, per Marco's own description

stops.name: Quinsai (Hangzhou), the city of heaven
stops.campa: Of every city the canon names, Quinsai (Hangzhou), capital once of the fallen Song, draws from Marco the longest and warmest chapter of all: a hundred miles around, twelve thousand bridges, some high enough for masted ships to pass beneath unstruck, a lake ringed with pleasure-boats and pavilions, ten great market squares thronged twice weekly, and streets so populous he will not set down the number for fear of being disbelieved. He calls it simply the greatest city in the world, and its name, which he renders 'city of heaven,' seems to him no exaggeration at all.
stops.quote: The city is beyond dispute the finest and the noblest in the world.
stops.quote_source: The Travels of Marco Polo, Book II, ch. LXXVI (Yule-Cordier translation)
suggested_refs: The West Lake of Hangzhou and its bridges, the 'city of heaven' of Marco's fondest chapter

stops.name: Zaiton (Quanzhou), the port of ships beyond counting
stops.campa: Zaiton, the great port of Manzi, is where Marco reckons the pepper trade of the whole world passes a hundredfold what reaches Alexandria for the Christian markets, an exaggeration, perhaps, but the harbor he describes is real enough: a forest of masts, junks loading porcelain and silk for India and the Arabian Sea, merchants of every nation come to buy and sell. He will return to this same port in a few years' time not as a trader but as an escort, when the Khan at last agrees to let the three Venetians go home by the only road that will still take them: the open sea.
stops.quote: It is one of the two greatest havens in the world for commerce.
stops.quote_source: The Travels of Marco Polo, Book II, ch. LXXXII (Yule-Cordier translation)
suggested_refs: The medieval port of Zaiton (Quanzhou), forest of masts and porcelain cargoes

segments.name: The Sea Road Home: Escorting the Princess

stops.name: Zaiton, departure with the Lady Kökötchin
stops.campa: An embassy from Arghun Khan of Persia asks Kublai for a bride of his own Mongol line; the choice falls on the young princess Kökötchin, and the overland roads west lie too torn by war for a bride's slow procession. The three Polos, homesick after two decades and lately fallen from favor with rivals at court, beg to escort her by sea and carry the Khan's leave to go home after. Thirteen four-masted ships with twelve sails apiece and six hundred souls put out from Zaiton in spring, the largest single fact of the whole return voyage, and Kublai's last great gift to the men who served him so long.
stops.quote: He then caused thirteen ships to be equipt, each of which had four masts, and often spread twelve sails.
stops.quote_source: The Travels of Marco Polo, Prologue, ch. XVIII (Yule-Cordier translation)
suggested_refs: The thirteen-ship fleet fitted out by Kublai Khan for Princess Kökötchin's escort

stops.name: Champa, the kingdom of pepper and elephants
stops.campa: The fleet coasts down past Champa, a rich kingdom of its own king and tongue, tributary to the Great Khan since Marco's own earlier embassy years helped settle the terms, he claims, though the chronology strains to fit. Elephants and lign-aloes wood are its wealth, and a court custom Marco records with plain wonder: that the king keeps three hundred and twenty-six wives and children beyond counting, and that no beautiful woman in the realm may marry until the king has had the first offer of her, a right he does not always take, but always holds by law.
suggested_refs: The kingdom of Champa on the Annam coast, tributary to the Great Khan

stops.name: Sumatra (Ferlec), five months waiting out the monsoon
stops.campa: The contrary monsoon pins the fleet five months at anchor off the island the canon calls Java the Less, Sumatra, long enough that Marco builds a stockaded camp ashore against the wilder tribes of the interior, whom he describes, not without relish, as eaters of their own kind's flesh and worshippers of whatever creature first crosses their path each morning. He counts eight separate kingdoms on the one island, each with its own king and tongue, and the strange fixed stars of a sky already tilting toward a hemisphere he has never before sailed under in his whole life.
stops.quote: They dug large ditches on the landward side to encompass the party, resting at either end on the sea-haven, and within these ditches they made bulwarks or stockades of timber for fear of those brutes of man-eaters.
stops.quote_source: The Travels of Marco Polo, Book III, ch. X (Yule-Cordier translation)
suggested_refs: The Polo fleet's stockaded camp on Sumatra, 'Java the Less' of the canon

stops.name: Ceylon, the isle of gems and Adam's Peak
stops.campa: Ceylon, smaller than its old fame but for Marco still the finest island of its size on earth, yields rubies, sapphires, topazes, and amethysts washed from its rivers, and a mountain the natives say holds the tomb of our first father Adam, which the Saracens venerate as much as the idolaters, a rare moment where Marco records three faiths reverencing the very same summit without contradiction troubling any of them. He prices a ruby he has seen at the local king's court beyond any gem the Great Khan himself possesses, high praise from a man who has stood inside Kublai's own treasury.
stops.quote: It has a compass of 2400 miles... You must know that rubies are found in this Island and in no other country in the world but this. They find there also sapphires and topazes and amethysts, and many other stones of price.
stops.quote_source: The Travels of Marco Polo, Book III, ch. XIV (Yule-Cordier translation)
suggested_refs: Adam's Peak (Sri Pada), Ceylon, venerated by Marco's account across three faiths at once

stops.name: Malabar coast, pepper, pearls, and the naked kings
stops.campa: Along the Malabar coast (Kayal's pearl-fishery, the pepper groves, the diamond and ginger markets), Marco catalogues kingdom after kingdom with the same close attention he gave the courts of Cathay: kings who go bare-chested and hung with jewels rather than robed, brahmins who will not kill so much as a fly, widows who leap living onto their husbands' pyres out of what the canon takes plainly as love and honor rather than compulsion. It is the last long coast before the strait to Persia, and the richest single stretch of ordinary trade goods he has catalogued since leaving Cathay behind him.
suggested_refs: The pearl-fishery of Kayal on the Malabar coast, per Marco's chapter on Maabar

stops.name: Hormuz: the princess delivered, the Khan Arghun dead
stops.campa: The fleet makes Hormuz at last with the princess Kökötchin still under the Polos' charge: six hundred souls sailed from Zaiton, a bare eight lived to see this harbor, so hard was the crossing, Marco says, though he and his own kin are all three still standing. Word meets them on the quay that Arghun Khan, for whom the bride was chosen, has been dead two years; his son Ghazan, campaigning on the frontier, will take her instead when he succeeds to the throne. The Polos hand her over to the regency and, their long charge discharged at last, turn overland for home.
stops.quote: When they embarked, they were in number some 600 persons, without counting the mariners; but nearly all died by the way, so that only eight survived.
stops.quote_source: The Travels of Marco Polo, Prologue, ch. XVIII (Yule-Cordier translation)
suggested_refs: The handover of Princess Kökötchin to the Ilkhanid regency at Hormuz

stops.name: Trebizond and Constantinople, the last leg of the world
stops.campa: From Persia the Polos ride the last long overland stage through Tabriz once more, across Greater Armenia and down to the Black Sea coast at Trebizond, then by ship on to Constantinople, the city where Nicolò and Maffeo had begun their whole adventure thirty-four years before as young merchants of the Latin quarter. Byzantine officials, the family later complains, relieve them of a portion of their remaining wealth in customs and outright extortion before they can take ship again for the Adriatic, a last, small robbery after surviving the length of Asia not once but twice over.
suggested_refs: The Latin quarter of Constantinople, where the Polo brothers' venture had begun in 1260

stops.name: Venice: the return, unrecognized at their own door
stops.campa: Twenty-four years gone, the three Polos come home in coarse Tartar dress, their Venetian speech gone rusty and strange, and their own kinsmen at the Corte del Milione do not know them and bar the door. It is only, family tradition tells, when they slit the seams of their patched and shabby coats and let cascades of rubies, sapphires, and pearls spill across the table that the household believes: these ragged Tartars are indeed Nicolò, Maffeo, and Marco Polo, richer than the doge, and the whole city that had given them up for dead spends the following days feasting the men it once mourned.
suggested_refs: The jewels ripped from the seams of the Polos' Tartar coats, per Venetian family tradition

segments.name: Curzola and the Prison of Genoa

stops.name: Curzola, captured in the sea-fight
stops.campa: Venice and Genoa are at open war again, and Marco, three years home, restless, perhaps commanding a galley of his own, sails with the Venetian fleet that meets the Genoese under Lamba Doria off the island of Curzola in the Adriatic. The battle goes hard against Venice: dozens of galleys sunk or taken, thousands of Venetians dead or captured, Marco among the prisoners marched off to Genoa in chains. It is the single worst defeat the Republic suffers in the long Genoese wars, and it delivers into Genoese hands, by the accident of one lost sea-fight, the one Venetian whose testimony will outlast every doge of his century.
suggested_refs: The Battle of Curzola (1298), where the Venetian fleet was broken and Marco captured

stops.name: Genoa: the prison, Rustichello, the book dictated
stops.campa: Held through the winter in the prison of the Palazzo di San Giorgio, Marco shares his cell with Rustichello of Pisa, a professional writer of romances taken prisoner on the war's other front, who recognizes in the Venetian's endless talk of Cathay and Cipangu and the Great Khan's court the richest unwritten book in Italy. Through the winter of 1298 into 1299 Marco dictates and Rustichello shapes it into Franco-Italian prose, part travel-report, part chivalric romance, until the manuscript called Il Milione, the Book of the Marvels of the World, exists: the ransom, in the end, that buys Marco lasting fame if not his liberty.
stops.quote: Since our Lord God did mould with his hands our first Father Adam, even until this day, never hath there been Christian, or Pagan, or Tartar, or Indian, or any man of any nation, who in his own person hath had so much knowledge and experience of the divers parts of the World and its Wonders as hath had this Messer Marco!
stops.quote_source: Il Milione / The Travels of Marco Polo, Prologue (Yule-Cordier translation)
suggested_refs: The Palazzo di San Giorgio, Genoa, where Il Milione was dictated to Rustichello da Pisa
sources: ancient-origins.net, 'The World Only Knows About Marco Polo Because of His Ghostwriter Prison Cell Mate'

segments.name: The Merchant Years and the Testament

stops.name: Venice, freed by the Peace of Milan
stops.campa: The Peace of Milan ends the Venetian-Genoese war in the summer of 1299 and releases the prisoners of Curzola on both sides; Marco comes home to the Corte del Milione a second time, already half-famous, for copies of the Genoa manuscript begin circulating in Italian, Latin, and Franco-Venetian within a few years, read as much for marvel as for fact. Venetians who cannot credit his numbers (a hundred thousand of this, a million of that) nickname him, half affectionately, Marco Milioni, and the courtyard where his family lives takes the name that survives to this day: Corte del Milion.
suggested_refs: The Corte del Milion, renamed for the nickname 'Marco Milioni' Venetians gave him

stops.name: Venice, marriage to Donata Badoer
stops.campa: Past forty-five, Marco marries Donata, daughter of the merchant Vitale Badoer, and the household in the Corte del Milione fills with the ordinary weather of Venetian domestic life after a quarter-century of desert and court: three daughters born in turn, Fantina, Bellela, and Moreta, none of whom will ever cross the sea their father crossed twice over. He resumes trade as a Venetian merchant of standing, invests in galleys and partnerships, sits on no great office, and is remembered by neighbors chiefly as a comfortable, talkative man who will not stop telling the same impossible stories about Cathay to anyone who will listen.
suggested_refs: Donata Badoer, wife of Marco Polo, and their three daughters Fantina, Bellela, and Moreta

stops.name: Venice, the merchant decades, and the doubters at the door
stops.campa: For two more decades Marco lives the unremarkable life of a Venetian man of business: lawsuits over a runaway slave, a partnership settling his uncle Maffeo's estate, small quarrels over inheritance with a cousin, while his book, copied and re-copied, spreads through the courts and countinghouses of Europe and gathers both fame and open scorn together. Visitors come to his door specifically to scoff at his numbers; the doubt follows him toward the grave and past it, so that within a decade of his death the chronicler Jacopo d'Acqui will already be setting down the deathbed scene as a settled piece of Venetian legend.
suggested_refs: The circulating manuscripts of Il Milione, read across Europe as marvel and disputed as fact
sources: jpost.com, '13th-century will reveals Marco Polo may have had a secret daughter'

stops.name: Venice, the will and the death
stops.campa: Ill and confined to his house, Marco dictates his last testament on the eighth of January, freeing a Tartar servant named Peter he had brought back from Cathay and leaving his estate to Donata and his three daughters; he dies within a day, on the eighth or ninth of January 1324, and is buried, tradition says, at the church of San Lorenzo, his grave later lost when the church was rebuilt. The legend that outlives the parchment has him ringed at the last by friends and a friar begging him to unsay his marvels and die shriven of exaggeration, and Marco refusing to the end: he has not told even half of what he saw.
stops.quote: I have not told half of what I saw, for I knew I would not be believed.
stops.quote_source: Attributed by tradition to Jacopo d'Acqui, Imago Mundi seu Chronica (c. 1330), the earliest recorded version of the deathbed legend
suggested_refs: Marco Polo's original 1323 will, held at the Biblioteca Nazionale Marciana, Venice
the deathbed legend of Il Milione, first recorded by Jacopo d'Acqui
sources: Jacopo d'Acqui, Imago Mundi seu Chronica (c. 1330)
